talks.title: Never a Better Time to Do a Startup

positions.claim: Startups founded today will be substantially more valuable and impactful than startups of previous eras, and the 'join a frontier lab or be an underclass' framing is wrong.
Startups win disproportionately when the technology landscape moves fast, costs fall, cycle times shorten, and incumbents lose their advantages — conditions all present in 2026.
AI fluency will beat many years of domain experience as a predictor of who builds successful companies.
Building the same startup as everyone else yields hype and easy fundraising but rarely produces the largest outcomes.
Being publicly dismissed for years was net-positive for OpenAI because it deterred serious competitors and bought research time.
Inability to find anyone who shares your contrarian belief is evidence you may be wrong; universal agreement is also a bad sign.
The advantage of doing YC over the next-best accelerator is larger now than it has ever been.
Moving to the Bay Area is still probably the best move for finding co-founders, though Altman says he has less intuition for this than he used to.
The hugging face incident was both an alignment failure and a security failure, and OpenAI made big mistakes that contributed to it.
Concentrating AI power in one company or model might buy short-term safety but would be a long-term disaster.
OpenAI should be reserved about imposing its own worldview on what people can build with AI, while still enforcing a minimum safety bar.
The next six months of model progress will feel roughly equivalent to the last two years of progress.
Worldwide inference demand will grow about 10x per year for many years, and 1000x per year sustained is not supportable.
Demand for sufficiently cheap, sufficiently high-quality intelligence is effectively uncapped, unlike electricity, so the compute shortage will effectively never end.
In roughly six and a half years the average person will use on the order of 500 billion tokens a month and the token leader quadrillions.
Year-over-year increases in individual freedom and agency are the right metric for whether the AI transition is going well.
An overreaction to AI safety producing abundance plus total surveillance is a serious dystopian risk, not just underreaction.
Publicly attacking people who are trying to build things is morally corrosive to the attacker and accomplishes nothing over time.
Being generally and unconditionally helpful to many people compounds into the relationships that later produce co-founders and companies.
A clear long-term vision paired with unclear first steps is characteristic of the best ambitious ideas, not a reason to lean out.
The tech industry is forgiving enough of early failure that founders should carry less anxiety than they do.
